newsitem.title: UK: Britain, Italy disagree on EU flexibility.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Italy disagree on EU flexibility.

text.p: Britain and Italy failed on Friday to bridge their differences on the crucial issue of whether a vanguard of European Union countries should be allowed to forge ahead faster than others.

Flexibility -- EU jargon for the concept of possible faster integration by some countries -- is shaping up as a major issue in talks on the future of the 15-nation bloc and was high on the agenda of a three-hour meeting between British Prime Minister John Major and his Italian counterpart, Romano Prodi.
Speaking to reporters later, Major said there was agreement within the EU on the need for flexibilty as the bloc expands to take in new members from eastern Europe.
But he said there was a range of views on what it should mean in practice.

France and Germany last year proposed writing a broad flexibility clause into the EU's treaty, with no country permitted a veto on others' plans to pool sovereignty. Italy, too, is not in favour of requiring unanimity.
But Britain, in a position reiterated by Major on Friday, insists that all countries must approve any plans for a group of EU members to push on without the others.

"I don't think anyone wishes to see a position in which a small hard core, against the interests of everybody else, proceed ahead. We need to find a way of coping with that and protecting the interests of other nations," he said.

Major said he had a better understanding of Italy's position after the talks but no compromise acceptable to all the EU was yet in sight. The issue is due to come to a head when the current inter-governmental conference on how to make the bloc work more effectively wraps up in Amsterdam in June.
"I think we made some interesting progress in discussing the problem but I wouldn't pretend to you that we cracked the problem in our discussion on flexibility," he said.
The two leaders also agreed to disagree on the EU's planned single currency.

Italy is striving mightily to meet the currency's tough eligibility criteria while Major, whose Conservative party is deeply split on the question, is taking a wait-and-see approach but doubts the project can safely start on time in 1999.
"There is a different history, a different interest, and I think this conversation -- even if the result is not similar action -- is very useful to understand each other much better," Prodi said.

Major praised Prodi for taking courageous decisions to prepare Italy for monetary union and said the two had agreed that the eligibility criteria, including tight budget, debt and inflation yardsticks, should not be watered down.
The two men said Anglo-Italian relations were in excellent shape and they had agreed to deepen cooperation in the area of defence manufacturing. They gave no details.
